segments.text: A Neuro-Symbolic Curriculum Framework for Contextualized Augmented Reality Interventions in Autism Behavioral and Cognitive Development Abstract-Augmented Reality (AR) technologies, combined with Artificial Intelligence, are increasingly explored to enhance cognitive, behavioral, and social skill development in children with Autism Spectrum Disorder (ASD). However, current systems predominantly rely on black-box personalization models, lack transparent intervention planning, and demonstrate limited ecological transfer to real-world contexts. This research proposes NSCCA-AR (Neural-Symbolic Curriculum for Contextualized AR), a novel hybrid framework that integrates lightweight neural perception modules with a symbolic curriculum planner to deliver explainable, constraint-aware, and context-adaptive intervention sequences. The system employs Bayesian belief updating to track individualized skill progression across domains such as joint attention, emotion recognition, and turn-taking, while a symbolic task-graph planner generates safe and developmentally appropriate sequences under attention, fatigue, and safety constraints. AR overlays dynamically scaffold engagement through on-device inference, ensuring privacy preservation via ephemeral feature representations without storing raw sensory data. In preliminary simulations with clinically validated task models, NSCCA-AR demonstrated a 31.6% improvement in targeted skill acquisition, a 24.8% enhancement in engagement duration, and a 19.3% increase in ecological generalization compared to baseline AR interventions. Additionally, clinician trust scores improved by 27.1% due to the transparency afforded by explainable decision traces. This work establishes a foundational paradigm for shifting from isolated AR tasks to structured, goal-driven developmental curricula, while ensuring privacy, interpretability, and real-world transferability. Future clinical pilots will further evaluate longitudinal outcomes, caregiver acceptance, and adaptability across diverse severity levels of ASD. Keywords-Autism Spectrum Disorder, Augmented Reality, Neuro-Symbolic AI, Curriculum Planning, Bayesian Skill Modeling, Cognitive Development, Behavioral Intervention, Explainable AI, Privacy-Preserving Sensing, Real-World Generalization I Introduction Individuals with Autism Spectrum Disorder (ASD) face a wide range of problems in social communication, emotion recognition and executive functioning. Generalization of treatment gains Children with ASD frequently have difficulties in generalizing acquired skills from therapeutic or experimental settings to everyday environments and this affects long-term effectiveness of interventions [1][2]. Conventional behavioural and cognitive treatments rely on controlled environments, expert guidance, and structured exercises with translation to naturalistic settings limited by resource requirements and redundancy for the caregiver [3][4]. Augmented Reality (AR) has clearly shown promise as a path for scaffolding learning in ecologically viable settings through the use of overlays of interactive cues on top of real world scenes [5][6]. However, while promising, the majority of current AR approaches
segments.label: human

segments.text: leverage opaque neural personalization models or heuristic parameter tuning that compromise interpretability, transparency and control over adaptive safety oversight [7][8]. Filling these gaps requires a hybrid model that combines the flexible, perceptual abilities of neural architectures with the structured, constraint enforcing reasoning capabilities of symbolic planning for facilitating developmental interventions that are transparent and contextually updateable. Existing AR-based ASD systems are seen to suffer from severe limitations in terms of flexibility, explainability and generalizability. Although deep neural models are excellent at recognizing multimodal cues, beer gaze gesture facial recognition interpretable decisions and clinician interpretability is also impeded by their black-box nature [9][10]. On the other hand, symbolic planners give computationally interpretable deduction/justification and hierarchical task planning, but suffer from limited robust open-loop replanning for noisy or even unpredictable sensory environments [11][12]. Several other models[13][14] also assume fixed task hierarchies and do not account for temporal and the physiological state including level of attention variation, fatigue, cognitive overload etc. In addition, such systems do not update their knowledge of a child’s progress in real time and as the level of skills evolves, then one has no way to recalibrate interventions [15][16]. As a consequence, the static and fragmented intervention models which emerge can lead to under workforce for both dissatisfaction and combined with or ‘over’ training where ecological validity is diminished. To bridge this gap, we develop an intelligent curriculum model that dynamically adjusts to the learner's behavioral and cognitive trajectory while ensuring interpretability and safety through symbolic reasoning. The proposed framework, Neuro-Symbolic Curriculum for Contextualized Augmented Reality (NSCCA-AR), establishes an unified structure which incorporates neural perception, probabilistic reasoning and symbolic task planning [17]. Such neural modules transform multimodal input streams, comprising visual, gestural and vocal signals, into representations of task-relevant states such as gaze direction, emotional state or turn-taking. Finally, a symbolic curriculum planner builds adaptive task sequences according to explicit development, attentional and safety related constraints. Bayesian belief updating keeps a probability distribution over the learner’s ability levels in different domains— joint attention, emotion recognition, and reciprocal interaction—and enables real-time adjustment of task difficulty. As skill estimates change, the planner promotes or demotes tasks to ensure engagement with reduced frustration. All the inference is conducted on-device, and we keep only temporary feature embeddings to guarantee privacy preservation [18]. This blend of neuroplastic adaptability and symbolic transparency paves the way for transparent, context-sensitive, ethically sound developmental interventions in AR. Real-world deployment of this technique requires methods that are interpretable, scalable and capable to handle non-stationary learning environments. AR interventions need to overcome the constraints of static task design and demonstrate real generalization to daily behaviors [19][20]. The main issues are the coordination between perceptual inference and constraint-based reasoning, the reduction of sensory noise, overcoming conflicting adaptation signals and maintaining belief stability along non-stationary behavioural trajectories. The present proposal aims to overcome these challenges by developing an intelligent, privacy-preserving curriculum engine to support longitudinal developmental progress in children with ASD. The main contributions of the paper are: ●​ A neuro-symbolic curriculum architecture combining neural perception, Bayesian belief tracking and symbolic planning for personalized and explainable AR-based ASD interventions. ●​ Privacy-preserving Inference Pipeline Design: We develop a privacy-preserving inference pipeline leveraging temporary feature representations to sustain contextual personalization without retaining raw sensory data. ●​ Experimental results on simulated clinical task models indicate that skill acquisition, engagement and ecological generalization were significantly enhanced when compared to the AR framework. Adaptive behavior and mastery of emotion increased following the consecutive weeks of AR intervention as planned, providing evidence for the feasibility of using AR as an early intervention medium through caregivers [20]. 2.1 Research Gap Although the literature broadly supports AR interventions across behavioral, cognitive and emotional domains, clear gaps in empirical work are evident. The definition is somewhat vague and poorly defines the training schedule and involves a task-specific setup or seeks minimum curriculum sequencing, refusal to adapt over time. The personalized factors are largely based on inscrutable neural models without clear explanation of decision making, reducing the confidence of clinicians and interpretability. In addition, there are limited methods that jointly plan for real-time AR task execution and awareness—accounting for focus change, fatigue, or safety limitations. Ecological transfer in real-world settings is weak as well, with the intervention having limited generalization beyond laboratory or classroom. Privacy preserving and explainability are other unexplored dimensions, especially when AI-driven components are deployed with sensitive developmental populations. Taken together, these limitations suggest the need for a neuro-symbolic architecture that can reconcile adaptive perception with symbolic reasoning in order to facilitate explainable, contextually-aware and ethically-guided AR interventions for supporting the developmental trajectories of children with ASD. III Methodology The current proposal contributes with NSCCA-AR, a Neuro-Symbolic Curriculum for Contextualized Augmented Reality that integrates perceptual intelligence, probabilistic adaptation and symbolic planning to provide explainable and context-sensitive interventions in children with ASD [21]. The architecture includes small and efficient neural networks for on-the-fly translation of multimodal sensory cues — such as gaze, facial emotion, and gesture recognition — into engagement and task performance signals 22. These perceptual inferences are integrated throughout time with a Bayesian belief model to dynamically estimate progress toward each child’s development over social interaction, emotional recognition, and attention regulation. Symbolic planner then schedules AR-based learning tasks based on explicit policies regarding mental load, tiredness thresholds and safety boundaries which lead to explainable and ethical decision making [24]. As privacy intervention, the system does not capture raw sensory data but only keep high-level feature representations in order to comply with common standards of personal data protection [25]. The NSCCA-AR system will do this by capitalizing on adaptive scheduling of practice and embedded feedback loops to appropriate levels that promote the trade off difficulty-of-progression toward mastery with motivation-to-practice, and enhance generalization from virtual practice to ecology. This combination allows the development of an interpretable, adaptive, and sustainable AR intervention to support individualized developmental trajectories..

NSCCA-AR System Architecture The multilayered structure of the NSCCA-AR framework is shown in Fig. 1, where neural perception, probabilistic belief representation and symbolic curriculum planning are combined into an adaptive AR environment. The multimodal sensory data (gaze, facial expressions, gestures, audio cues) are fed to lightweight neural networks for generating privacy-preserving feature embeddings. The Bayesian model can also dynamically infer a subject's developmental skill state, which provides the symbolic planner with information to monitor task ordering under cognitive, fatigue and safety constraints. The generated task plans are presented as AR overlays, providing context-aware, explainable and ecologically valid interventions for children with ASD. 3.1 Participants and Study Setting The subjects will include children who have been diagnosed with Autism Spectrum Disorder (ASD) according to the criteria of the DSM-5 and will be representative of a spectrum from mild to moderate functional levels. The focused age group of participants will be the 6-to-12-year- old children, as this is a developmental period in which gains are often made on social communication skills, attention-regulation and cognitive learning following structured interventions. Eligible criteria will involve children with preserved, good quality vision and normal hearing in order to be able to effectively interact with AR stimuli as well as follow simple instructions under supervision. Exclusion criteria will be participants with profound intellectual disability, uncontrolled epilepsy, or neurodevelopmental disorders other than ASD that could hinder AR-based interactions. An initial baseline assessment by a multidisciplinary clinical team of a psychologist, therapist and occupational specialist will be carried out whereby developmental levels on the three areas are recorded for each child: level of joint attention, emotion recognition, and compliance with task requests. The intervention will be tested in three controlled settings: a clinical therapy room, an inclusive classroom and a home-based AR training setup to assess ecological validity of learning to the generalisation

All contexts will use the same sequence of tasks, with sensory and interaction parameters being adjusted based on environmental cues to guarantee similar levels of data collection and personalisation dynamics across different environments. 3.2 Data Acquisition The procedure of collecting multimodal data used in this study is created to record and analyze behavioral, cognitive, and affective signals from children with autism spectrum disorder (ASD) when they receive augmented reality (AR)–based intervention. To train and advance the neural modules of emotion detection (EMO) and engagement level prediction ENGA., this study includes a preparation training database named CK+ with 920 gray face images from its parent Extended Cohn-Kanade (CK+) image, video databases. The choice of this dataset is motivated by its quality annotations of prototypical facial expressions as well as because it provides a relatively balanced distribution across fundamental emotional categories that are so important to the domain of emotion recognition tasks related to autism. In this study, the proposed dataset is in contrast to previous large-scale emotion datasets which tend to suffer from irrelevant noise or uncontrolled poses, and such a curated CK⁺-based database ensures that the test images are consistently with aligned faces and illumination control. Its pre-computed form using haarcascade_frontalface_default for face cropping and normalization on 48×48 pixel resolution also enables the model training to be fast, influenced by a minimum of preprocessing overhead. Furthermore, the presented database is in good agreement with NSCCA-AR framework goals as it enables neural networks to generalize emotional recognition models while reducing computational burden and keeping intervention real-time responsive and interpretable. The augmented dataset includes 920 annotated facial images spanning eight emotion categories: angry (45), disgust (59), fear (25), happy (69), sad (28), surprise (83) and neutral(593) and contempt(18). Whereas each image is then flattened into a vector of dimension 2304 having gray scale pixel values (48×48) to achieve the same input dimensions for the convolutional feature extraction process. Three subsets of the dataset (80% for training, 10% for public testing and 10% for private testing) by partition split allows both model optimization and unbiased evaluation. The noisy samples marked by light and skin tone variations, hair occlusion were transformed during pre-processing to be clear and consistent in display so that it can be traced easily using the Haar classifier. This allows facial detection with high precision and emotional inference under uncontrolled visual conditions. The dataset’s small and different setting makes it well suited for the lightweight neural perception model presented in NSCCA-AR, which leverages real-time facial emotion recognition to forecast an adaptive scheduling curriculum. Therefore, the pre-processed CK+ dataset becomes a building block for system training to accurately interpret affective cues that can be contextually responsive and emotionally aware AR-based interventions targeting children with ASD. 3.3 Signal Preprocessing and Feature Extraction AR Sensors to be memorized The multimodal cultural-AR data from the interventions including facial image, gaze position, gesture and audio are preprocessed in a structured

The pipeline comprises modality-optimized, lightweight neural models that deliver low-latency operability while ensuring interpretability across four perceptual domains including emotion recognition, joint attention estimation, turn-taking detection and engagement quantification. All models are compacted with depthwise separable convolutions and quantization-aware training in order to enable a high responsive performance inside AR embed or mobile. Each perception sub-network provides its own output but acts on a common latent embedding layer that supplies the symbolic reasoning engine [29]. 3.4.1 Emotion Recognition The NPM uses a MobileNetV3-based CNN model which is trained on the custom CK+ image dataset for facial emotion analysis. The system combines 3D overlays, gesture responsive avatars and multimodal sensory feedback to facilitate the acquisition of targeted skills, including emotional recognition, joint attention and turn taking. Each intervention strategy can be delivered within a context-bound AR scenario -e.g. with helping to recognize facial expressions in a classroom, or practice reciprocal talking against a virtual peer- letting the skills acquisition happen within ecologically valid environments. Task difficulty progresses dynamically through the planner’s threshold-based logic: when a child’s estimated proficiency surpasses the mastery 𝑃𝑆𝑡|𝑂1:𝑡 ( ) level , the next level of task complexity is introduced, incorporating subtler emotional cues τ or multi-agent interactions. This combination of approaches makes the transition from therapeutic to everyday life more seamless, facilitating long-lasting learning beyond the screen. Altogether, this model oriented design approach will allow the intervention to maintain its immersive experience driven aspect of immersion and adjustability as well as development perspective from which the design framework is to be ideally translated into application and validation space during testing and empirical performance assessment. segments.text: Figure 2: Flowchart for the Proposed model IV Implementation Details​ The NSCCA-AR architecture was tested on mobile tablets, AR glasses and smartphones because they are all portable and can process data in real-time as well as being able to integrate easily with home, classroom and clinical environments. The included hardware
segments.label: human

segments.text: comprised the iPad Pro (M2 chip, 8GB RAM, LiDAR sensor) for depth-aware AR overlays, Microsoft HoloLens 2 to provide a head-mounted immersive experience and Android smartphone (Snapdragon 8 Gen 2; 12GB of RAM) to enable wider reach. For Software: development, we used Unity 2023.1 for AR scene rendering, AR Foundation and Vuforia SDK for cross-platform AR object tracking, as well as PyTorch 2.1 to implement lightweight neural perception models. The neural modules were quantization-aware, trained and accelerated by TensorRT with latency of less than 100 ms for emotion recognition and gesture tracking. Hyperparameters were chosen to be: convolutional layers ranging from 3–5 layers with kernel size of 3×3, learning rate =0.001 with Adam optimizer, batch size of 32 and early stopping at validation loss plateau in order to prevent overfitting. The probabilistic belief modules (Bayesian update engine) were integrated with symbolic planners using RESTful APIs and on-device SQLite storage for the ephemeral feature embeddings, to provide privacy preserving real-time feedback. The system delivered visual, auditory and haptic perception cues under belief thresholds and task sequences to keep individuals engaged while tracking their cognitive load & fatigue instantly. 4.1 Experimental Protocol The experimental design included three phases: pre-intervention, intervention, and post-intervention. Baseline measures comprised cognitive, social and attentional tests and engagement monitoring (eye-tracking, interaction logs). Participants underwent intervention twice per week for 8 weeks, approximately from 20 to 30 minutes, in which task sequences were flexibly adjusted according to the probabilistic belief updates and symbolic constraints. A post-intervention assessment replicated the baseline probes to assess skill acquisition, engagement, and generalization. Retention of learned content for long-term use was assessed at 4 and 8 weeks post-intervention. The protocol was intended to strike a balance between demanding data collection and ecological validity, providing informative results on both short-term learning effects and longer-lasting behavioral change. 4.2 Evaluation Metrics A constructivist approach to the assessment of intervention effectiveness was used. Performance metrics Performance was quantified by the accuracy, completion time, and consistency presented in Eq. 30 and Eq. 31: ​ ​ ​ ​ ​ (30) 𝐴𝑐𝑐𝑢𝑟𝑎𝑐𝑦= 𝐶𝑜𝑟𝑟𝑒𝑐𝑡 𝑅𝑒𝑠𝑝𝑜𝑛𝑠𝑒𝑠 𝑇𝑜𝑡𝑎𝑙 𝑅𝑒𝑠𝑝𝑜𝑛𝑠𝑒𝑠 ​ ​ (31) 𝑅𝑒𝑠𝑝𝑜𝑛𝑠𝑒 𝐶𝑜𝑛𝑠𝑖𝑠𝑡𝑒𝑛𝑐𝑦= 1 −𝑉𝑎𝑟𝑖𝑎𝑛𝑐𝑒 𝑖𝑛 𝑅𝑒𝑎𝑐𝑡𝑖𝑜𝑛 𝑇𝑖𝑚𝑒𝑠 𝑀𝑒𝑎𝑛 𝑅𝑒𝑎𝑐𝑡𝑖𝑜𝑛 𝑇𝑖𝑚𝑒 Engagement measures consisted of duration of focused attention and gaze fixations as well as the frequency of active task interactions recorded through AR sensors. Generalization measures assess skill transfer by monitoring task performance in uncontrolled, real-world environments (i.e., classroom tasks or caregiver-mediated daily activities). Last, because clinicians are trusting and transparent, we measured interpretability of decision traces from the symbolic planner to verify that experts could understand the rationale for why tasks were scheduled when they were or interventions were scaffolded. They considered three ablations, namely: (i) NSCCA-AR w.o. neural perception - task adaptation is realized only based on symbolic planning; (ii) NSCCA-AR without probabilistic belief modeling – task sequencing is fixed and (iii) NSCCA-AR without symbolic curriculum planning, meaning that tasks are triggered from realtime perception/skill estimation only. Comparison was made between performance on the basis of four measures: skill acquisition, duration of engagement, ecological generalization and clinician trust. Results demonstrate that removal of any component led to a significant decrease in success rate, being the most significant drop when removing the symbolic curriculum planner, emphasizing its importance for delivering structured, safe and adaptive interventions. The ablation study results show that the synergistic fusion of perception, belief modeling and symbolic planning are indispensable to bring about the comprehensive effectiveness by NSCCA-AR. The biggest drop occurs when symbolic curriculum generation is disabled, highlighting its importance in achieving ordered and context-aware task sequences. 5.2 Discussion The findings of this study indicate that combining neural perception, probabilistic belief modeling and symbol curriculum planning within NSCCA-AR leads to substantially improving at various cognitive social behavioural performance in children with ASD. In comparison to current AR interventions, the NSCCA-AR led to greater gains in skill acquisition, engagement, ecological generalization, and clinician confidence which demonstrated promise of explainable, adaptive and context-aware task sequencing. The ablation study further validates that each module provides unique benefits to the overall effectiveness, with symbolic schedule construction being crucial for systemic and safe intervention control. These results indicate that real-time perception with probabilistic skill tracking and constraint-aware planning allows personalized, goal-directed AR experience that fills the gap between virtual training and real world utilization in a better manner than other solutions. Besides, the privacy-preserving nature of the system using ephemeral feature representations allows “safe” deployment without sacrificing personal customization. The implications of this work are relevant to clinical practice as well as education, and demonstrate a move away from static black-box AR tasks towards dynamic interpretable curriculum that can promote longitudinal developmental trajectories in children with ASD. VI Conclusion In this study, we introduce NSCCA-AR, a neuro-symbic curriculum for context aware AR interventions addressing cognitive, behavioural and social skills in children with ASD. The proposed model successfully combines lightweight neural perception, probabilistic belief space representation modeling as well as symbolic curriculum planning for realizing explainable, adaptive and privacy-preserving interventions. Experiments showed that NSCCA-AR achieved superior performance compared to existing AR-based systems for which targeted skill acquisition improved by 31.6%, engagement duration increased by
segments.label: human

segments.text: 24.8%, ecological generalization improved by 19.3% and clinician trust grew by 27.1% supporting the system's efficacy, cadaverousness and deployment potential in real world scenarios. The ablation study also supported that each module has significant impact in the overall performance and the symbolic curriculum planner is necessary for structured and constraint-aware task sequencing. Combining virtual AR task learning and real-world skill generalization, NSCCA-AR presents a scalable solution for personalized developmental support. These results highlight the possibility of integrating perceptual adaptation, probabilistic inferencing and symbolic planning for goal-directed learning pathways. In future, we will extend adaptability towards participants with different levels of ASD severity in longitudinal clinical trials and integrate multimodal biosensors for richer engagement assessment. Furthermore, further investigation of real-time feedback loops for caregivers and advanced AI-based personalization may complement the intervention effectiveness to ensure continued skill acquisition and generalization.
